utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would expect you to concentrate today on the matters or time period that is covered by the indictment. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. In ten minutes' time we'll be in the 1990s, but before that, I'd like to inform you that I intend to send the Prosecution and the Chamber, Trial Chamber, to send from time to time a collection of so-called agreed fact lists so that we don't dispute and challenge elementary points. So the Prosecution can either reject or accept, but if we have this list, then that will help us. Now may we have 1D1409 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not on e-court I've been informed. Well, in that case let's put it on the ELMO. So may the witness be provided with a copy. I have a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you see this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a copy of it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see it on the overhead projector?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you see that that is what the Allies offered Serbia in 1915 in London?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask the provenance of this -- this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's from the documentation, the historical documents pertaining to the 1915 London Conference. Just tell me whether you agree or not. In your opinion, is that what this is, this is what it shows? And you should know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. You know nothing about what Serbia was offered in London. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on and have on e-court 1D1407 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's not what the witness said. What he said is he didn't know about this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And does Mr. Donia know -- or, Mr. Donia, do you know that in 1915 Serbia was offered not create Yugoslavia but to create Serbia and that these territories were offered to Serbia: Backa, Slavonia, Bosna, part of Dalmatia, and part of Albania which we can see on this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not certain that the map accurately reflects what was offered, but I would concur that approximately those lands were discussed at the conference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree after that with the Corfu Declaration that Serbia gave up on this and came out in favour of all south -- a state of all South Slavs except for the Bulgarians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On another occasion we'll be offering up the Corfu Declaration, but can I admit this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think Dr. Donia has addressed any aspect of this map whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's obvious, but does the Prosecution disagree that this map accurately sets out those territories which were on offer by the Allies in the 1915 conference in respect of the setting up of the state of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could answer that, Your Honour. To me that underscores the lack of relevance of this portion of the examination. You -- it's not an aspect of the case to which the Prosecution has devoted extensive attention. But to the extent that the Court considers that the witness's answer in some way provided a sufficient nexus to the document and accepts that the examination in that respect or the examination in that regard was relevant, then I think the guidelines would apply in their normal manner, but the relevance of this area of questioning has already and addressed, and I think the point's been made before. I don't think there's any major reason to spend time disputing this particular document, but if the Court is asking for the Prosecution's position on a relevant or marginally -- or on aspects of the case the Prosecution considers irrelevant or marginally irrelevant, that that won't assist the admissibility issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I was simply asking whether or not the map, as it is set out, is a map which is disputed by the Prosecution. Issues of relevancy can come later in the Tribunal's determination. I simply want to know whether this is a map which is disputed in the terms of its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness asked for provenance. We weren't given -- I didn't hear it provided in response. We're not aware of the provenance of this document, so we're not in a position to assist with regard to whether it accurately reflects the territories on offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the answer Judge Morrison wanted to hear. Mr. Karadzic, we are not satisfied as to the foundation of this map, and the witness was not able to confirm anything about it. We'll not admit it. You can tender it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say what the foundation for this is, Your Excellency. First of all, this London Agreement is mentioned in the intercepts. That's the first point. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has bee ruled. You will have another opportunity to tender it. Let's move on to the time period to which you're going to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more document, please, or, rather, yesterday, Mr. Donia said that he didn't know something about certain matters, and I should like to take five minutes or ten minutes to present the documents which are basic, elementary, without which we cannot discuss anything because these are all documents about the creation and disappearance in Yugoslavia, and the Bosnian crisis took place within the Yugoslav crisis, and Mr. Donia is speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Donia -- so we have to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- don't make a speech. Just directly go to your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D1407 next, please. On e-court, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Donia, that Yugoslavia was not created by the association of republics, them polling together?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The creation of the first joint state, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in most of the polities that became part of Yugoslavia were not republics, so I would agree that they were not created by an association of republics, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that by the same token it couldn't have become dissolved with the dissociation of the republics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe the first Yugoslavia had republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in 1991, President Kucan presented the thesis whereby Yugoslavia should develop with a disassociation of the republics, that is to say that Yugoslavia should disappear with the disassociation of the republics. Have you heard of that term, disassociation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking a point of constitutional interpretation that I'm really not qualified to answer and would note that it was heavily contested at the time as well. So I'm really not in a position to give you an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now look at page 151 of this same document, please. As you can see, Mr. Donia, this is a collection of documents on Yugoslavia and about Yugoslavia. Page 151 is the page I'd like displayed, please. In the document itself, the document page. So it's just a collection of documents. These aren't documents written by anybody or authored by anybody. They're a collection of documents about Yugoslavia. 151 is the page I'd like us to look at, please. Thank you. It's rather a poor copy, but this is what it says -- may somebody -- could the usher hand this to Mr. Donia, please. I think this is a better copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think we can manage if you take a look at the monitor. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll have to read it out then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] National Council of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs declares the unification of the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs, created on the territory of the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy with the Kingdom of Serbia and Montenegro in the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Now, do you now agree that this is a fact that we were not able to agree upon yesterday, that the -- the state of the Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs did exist west of the Drina River and that it is that state that united with the Kingdom of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It, I guess, lasted seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now have 163, page 163, displayed, please, of that same document. It's page 88 on e-court. Well, actually, it's chapter 67, "Treaty." "[In English] The treaty of peace between the principal allied and associated powers and the Serb-Croat-Slovene state." [Interpretation] Let's take a look at what it says lower down: "[In English] Whereas the Serbs, Croats, and Slovene peoples of the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy have of their own free will determined to unite with Serbia in a permanent union for the purpose of forming a single sovereign independent state under the title of Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes." [Interpretation] Does that say quite clearly, and this is a treaty, an international covenant, agreement, it's history, the history of the creation of Yugoslavia. And can you see from this that the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes from the former Austro-Hungary became peoples, constituent peoples, on a territory on a footing of equality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the -- the rest of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The document is the whole book. It's on e-court, and you can look at all of it. I had actually expected that you would bear this in mind, because you're our most important expert in these matters, after all, but let's move on to the next page so that Mr. Donia can have a look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. The book is a very diverse collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is titled as "Yugoslavia Through Documents."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I mean for your purposes, wouldn't it suffice simply if the witness agrees, and he may or may not, that after the west kingdom of Serbia had formed a new country with the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbia, was it then connected with the Kingdom of Serbia on the 1st of December of 1918, thereafter being named the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and in 1918 as a result of that Serbia was recognised as a state by the rest of the world in its own entity really for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, no, that's not how it was. The crux of the matter is that the territories which until 1918 were within Austro-Hungary were constituted into a state of three peoples, the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, or, rather, Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, and it is that state which became united with Serbia which existed ever since the Berlin Congress as an independent state. So the crux of the matter is that the Serbs west of the Drina River and along the Danube, the Serbs from Austro-Hungary were equal to the Slovenes and Croats and equal owners of that state. They have their statehood rights, and it is that state which became united with Serbia. The main point of the matter is that it was a state. It doesn't matter how long it lasted. It was able to conclude international agreements, and it became united into a new state, but it is a state, and the Serbs there were a constituent people, and they had -- they had their state rights. And if Mr. Donia can confirm that, we can move on and needn't dwell on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with Your Honour's formulation of what I can affirm, which is that the Kingdom of Serbia, through it's proclamation of 1 December 1918, in fact, declared the creation of a new polity known as the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and a -- the representatives that we have been seeing here formed first as the Yugoslav committee and then for this very fleeting period of about seven days having declared themselves a state were parties to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thereafter, whatever one names it, it was recognised as a state and had the rights and attributes of a state including, for instance, negotiating treaties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic is right as to that. So whatever we call it, let's not argue about the names, that's really the pivotal period and perhaps Dr. Karadzic can move on from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was wrong in the transcript. Serbia itself, Serbia proper, the Kingdom of Serbia existed as an independent state from the Berlin Congress; whereas, the state of Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs lasted for a short period of time, but it was a state nonetheless and it became united. Now, in the transcript it says that that state, Slovenes, Croats, and Serbs lasted from the Berlin Congress. The Kingdom of Yugoslavia was independent from the Berlin Congress and it became associated with this other state. Now, if we've dealt with that we can move on. And I'd like to tender all these documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karadzic. All these documents? We looked at page 1051 and some more pages. You referred to those -- those pages we've looked at.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 151, page 151 of this collection of documents, 163 is the next page I'd like to tender. Well, we can look at 168 as well. And 168. It also refers to the unification of those states. Well can we have 168 called up, please. It's a very important page. 168 of the same document. Page 90 on e-court. That's right. Article 12. "[In English] Pending the conclusion of new treaties or conventions, all treaties, conventions, agreements, and obligations between Serbia, on one hand, and any of the principal Allied and Associated Forces -- Powers, on the other hand, which were in force on the -- August the 1st, 1914, or which have since been entered into shall -- shall ipso facto be binding upon the Serb-Croat-Slovene State." [Interpretation] Therefore, Serbia was bringing into that new state all its state duties and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. This -- this states simply that the agreements that were in force as of 1 August 1914 would pass to the -- the kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. There obviously would be some commitments to Serbia or possibly other agreements entered into after 1 August 1914 which would not pass to the new state according to this -- this provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it simply says that pending conclusion of new treaties, all treaties, conventions, agreements, and obligations between Serbia and the principal Allied and Associated Powers which were in force as of 1 August 1914 or which have since entered into shall ipso facto be binding upon the state. So there may have been agreements that were -- things that were promised to Serbia that were not formally entered into as agreements that did not pass. The entire -- I don't think that you can say from this that the entire state character of the Kingdom of Serbia passed to the new state. It may have by some internal agreement, but that's not what this says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But one should understand this in the following way: That in future, it won't be Serbia concluding agreements but the new state and everything that Serbia had concluded before that. So the latter part of what you said is correct, but it says pending the conclusion of new treaties. So after this. Serbia will longer conclude treaties alone, but it will be the new state that will do that. Now I'd like to tender those three pages, Your Excellencies, into evidence. Well, we can look at another page perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm just wondering how relevant this is to our case. Ms. Edgerton, are you opposing to the admission of these three pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, but the document that Dr. Karadzic was excerpting from actually runs from pages 163 to 169. So these three pages are part of one document. If the Trial Chamber does deem it relevant, it might be useful for them to have the whole document so pages 163 to 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do so. Mr. Karadzic, let's move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these pages will be Exhibit D244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have page 206 and then 207 straight after that, please. It's 110 on e-court and that's the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the date is 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- let's come to the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, just cast your eye on that document. The republics are being created there and that's very important. It's pivotal. Let's see what republics and what peoples. So just a little patience, three more minutes. So the republics are being created here in Jajce. Is Jajce an important place, Mr. Donia, for understanding the Yugoslav crisis? AVNOJ, the Anti-Fascist Council of National Liberation and its session in Jajce, AVNOJ as it was called.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's terribly important in terms of the dissolution of Yugoslavia. It's certainly important in terms of the formation of socialist Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which existed under a number of other names prior to 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was 1979. But do you agree, Mr. Donia, that the AVNOJ borders were the main topic during the dissolution of Yugoslavia, that it was the AVNOJ borders that were disputed? The disputes were all about the AVNOJ borders; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were referenced as the AVNOJ borders, but in many cases I think they were actually drawn well after the conference in Jajce and after that time that this document was generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree. Can we move down, down 97 where it says "Decision to create Yugoslavia on the Federal Principles." Number 79. Down, a bit, please. And may we turn to the next page. Item 2 on the following page. At the top. Thank you. Yes. "[In English] In order to carry out the principle of sovereignty of the peoples of the Yugoslavia, and in order for Yugoslavia to present a true homeland for all its peoples and never again to become a domain of any other hegemonistic clique, Yugoslavia is building and will be built along the lines of the federal principles which will provide for full equality of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, Macedonians, and Montenegrins, respectively the principles [sic] of Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] Are there five peoples mentioned there, Mr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There, I think, actually five named, and then the door is opened for peoples that are not named in the very final phrase of the -- of the Resolution. I think it's worth noting that this formulation follows the model of Soviet nationality theory from the Stalinist era which used these terms like "hegemonistic clique" and "constituent peoples" or "sovereignty of peoples," and some of that is shared with other systems as well, but this document really, I think amply shows the origins of this type of formulation in Stalinist nationality theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said fully, Mr. Donia. Is part of human rights the right to national feelings? Does a group have the right to have national rights, peoples rights, group rights?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to clarify, my comment was that the provenance of this language and this document comes much more from Soviet nationality theory than it does from the western democratic tradition of rights of nations or international human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not going to debate that. I agree that AVNOJ was not a democratic body, but we lived under this AVNOJ. At this point in time, though, Mr. Donia, what do you think? What is the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1943, when this was being created.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina? Probably somewhere around 2.5 to 3 million people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in terms of ethnicity, who are they?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to accept the term "ethnicity" as the primary group identification, I would say that the population was a mixture of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and some Yugoslavs and some other peoples including Roma, Slovenes, Albanians, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any Yugoslavs then? Did they exist as a category in 1943?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you immediately come across the question of how we know what -- what they were, and the answer is, of course, we really don't -- didn't have a census until 1948 in the socialist period, and the last census in the kingdom -- or in Royal Yugoslavia, I think, was 1930, '34, something like that, before the Second World War. So the fact is what the composition was at that time really isn't knowable. The best we could do is go to the 1948 census, and recognising that the 1948 census, like every census, limits or recognises only certain responses in counting people that -- that would be the best we could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that that census of 1948 was affected by the suffering of the Serbs during the course of the Second World War? You admitted to about 100.000, so we'll go back to that later, but do you agree that in 1948 the number of Serbs was smaller than it would have been otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I admitted to 100.000. I -- just -- going back to the antecedent to your question there, I don't recall making that statement. I think the -- I would agree that the census of 1948 was affected by the suffering of all individuals and peoples during the course of the Second World War and certainly was profoundly affected by the suffering of the Jews and also -- I mean, I think every group that we think of as a nation today suffered substantially during the course of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's correct what you said about the Jews, that is, but do you accept that it was the Serbs who suffered the most during the Second World War and that genocide was committed against the Serbs then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept the first part of your question, that it was the Serbs that suffered the most, no. I concur that genocide was committed against the Serbs in the course of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can you admit these two pages, 206 and 207, and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, we'll admit it. But what's the practice? If we admit part of the book it will be added to the originally admitted part. So that is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It can be admitted also as Exhibit D244, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Is 1D1408. That's what I'd like us to have a look at now, from 4721 to 4807. We are going to play this, and let's hear what Lord Carrington has to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will agree, won't you, that it was Lord Carrington who chaired the first conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were actually notified about this item when we came into the courtroom, so perhaps it's appropriate that this be played later, because I wouldn't think that notification the moment we step into the courtroom is actually sufficient notification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a well-known film. It's well-known footage, but all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. How long would you need to prepare? Just if it is to be played at the end of today's session would it be okay for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can have a look at it over the break, Your Honour, but I simply haven't had an opportunity until this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I would like to put a few things to you, and if you agree, we don't have to prove them any further. And if you say that this is not the case, then I'm going to try to prove it later on. Do you agree that in Yugoslav practice, in Yugoslav constitutional practice, there are peoples and national minorities, and later on they were called nationalities as you noted as well, and you observed that, too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- in Yugoslav theory, nationality theory, if you will, yes, there were nations, nationalities, and national minorities, and the -- and that -- that spoke to -- and there was a hierarchy, the top rung being the nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that peoples are those whose homeland Yugoslavia is, and national minorities are those who have their mainstream state, as it were, somewhere in the neighbourhood? Well, not necessarily in the immediate neighbourhood. Say Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of Yugoslav nationality theory that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that Yugoslavia is the main state, the mother state of Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Muslims, Macedonians, Montenegrins, and Yugoslavs? Do they have their own national state anywhere else but in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's two questions. I agree that you have named the nations that have their principal homeland in Yugoslavia, on Yugoslav territory, and none of those nations have a national state or had a national state outside of Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you agree that these seven categories are not national minorities. Rather, they are state creating peoples of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of Yugoslav nationality theory, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that my last political endeavour had been in 1968, in the student movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that up until 1990 I was a silent dissident who was involved in psychiatry first and foremost, but then also literature and sports as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't know how much of a dissident you were. I would agree with the rest of your formulation. You were involved in psychiatry first and foremost. You were an accomplished poet and also involved in coaching or counselling a sports team. So, yeah, I agree with that part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to tell you about all the things that happened from when I stopped being politically involved until I went back into politics. As for November 1968, do you agree that the Albanians in Kosovo started celebrating the national holiday of the Albanian flag? So that was a different state altogether. And they were celebrating that holiday on the territory of Yugoslavia this. Only requires a yes or no, nothing more than that. I mean, we will provide further proof, if necessary, later on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 15th of March, 1969, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, the only political party and the ruling political party, introduced the principle of parity? That is to say that its organs consisted of an equal number of representatives from each and every republic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically know that that's the -- I don't know that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that from the 14th up until the 17th of January, 1970, the tenth session of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Croatia was held and it laid the foundations for the so-called mass movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This mass movement, was it a separatist movement, a pre-eminently separatist and national movement? Not a national movement but a nationalist movement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was pre-eminently separatist, but there were certainly members of it or those who participated in it who held separatist views, but I -- and I don't want to make a distinction that you would like to make here between it being national and nationalist purely in terms of the English translation. I would call it a national movement in English and recognise that it was a flowering of democratic sentiment and of national sentiment on behalf of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that under the pressure exerted by that movement, on the 30th of June, 1971, amendments were adopted to the constitution of Yugoslavia, amendments from 20 up to 42. So it was amendments 20 through 42. Amendments to the constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically which number amendments were adopted. I certainly agree that amendments were adopted at about that time. And I'm -- I wouldn't say that they were adopted under the pressure exerted by Masbuk [phoen] but, rather, in response to the flowering of national sentiment in general at -- of a number of groups at that time and then concerns about the, let's say, unity and coherence of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did these amendments establish new relations between and among the republics and in this case the autonomous provinces within Serbia gained further importance as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are -- both questions are true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this the first time that Serbia became federalised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it became federalised, no. Again, it maybe is a question of constitutional law, but I wouldn't characterize it that way, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Josip Broz Tito, on the 1st and 2nd of December, 1971, in Karadjordjevo, put an end to the mass movement of the Croats and punished them all? Actually, he called for their resignations, and the entire top political echelon of Croatia was removed. They were declared nationalist, separatist, et cetera, and they were removed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all, but the general tenor of your question, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that again that Josip Broz Tito generated and carried out on the 26th of October, 1972, a removal of the Serbian leadership headed by Marko Nikezic and Latinka Perovic, having labeled them as the protagonists of a liberal policy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't attest to the date or the specifics of that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Croatian leadership was replaced as nationalist, whereas the Serb leadership was removed as neo-liberalist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how were Nikezic and Latinka Perovic removed? What was the label that was used in their case, and what pretext was resorted to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on the 21st of February, 1974, a new constitution was passed, a well known 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the specific date, but certainly would concur that a new constitution was passed in 1974, not only in the SF -- the SFRJ, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but also in each of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree that this constitution gave the autonomous provinces, Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia, practically the level of republics? They were -- they were declared constituent elements of the federation as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in this way Serbia was federalised; namely, that it could not pass laws and other legislation without the agreement of the Assemblies of Kosovo and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not -- the use of the word "federalised" here is to me problematic, and I can't agree simply because I don't know what you mean by -- by "federalised." And I know that over time you've meant a lot of different things by using the term "federal."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was only Serbia that had entities within it that it had to ask before it would carry out any changes in the territory of Serbia? And that is something that was not the case either in Croatia or in Slovenia, Macedonia, Montenegro, all the other republics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a matter of Yugoslav constitutional law, and I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Josip Broz Tito died on the 4th of May, 1980, or at least that is when this was made public?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept the date of 4 May 1980 as the date of his death, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Kosovo, on the 11th of March, 1981, large-scale demonstrations broke out under the slogan "Kosovo Republic"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on the 2nd of April, 1981, the Presidency of the SFRY passed a decision on martial law in Kosovo, and they also set up through the secretariat -- the Federal Secretariat for the interior units that were sent to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the specific date nor the specific content of the decision that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, martial law is a historical fact. Martial law is a historical fact. Because of what had happened in Kosovo, that is why it was declared. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not agreeing with your characterization simply because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I thought that you had to know about that because that was the beginning of the crisis. It's not even the beginning, for that matter. Do you agree that due to all of these developments Lazar Kolisevski, a high-ranking Macedonian official, revealed that the essence of the policy of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was contained in the slogan a weak Serbia means a strong Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You disagree or you simply don't know that he said that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know precisely what he said, nor do I know that it's purely because of those developments that -- that he made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Lazar Kolisevski?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Presidency, and I believe that after Tito's death he was the first president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was the representative Macedonia in the Presidency, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that on the 28th of September, 1989, the Assembly of Slovenia passed the first amendments out of a series of amendments to the republican constitution, thus initiating a process of moving away from the Yugoslav Federation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree or do you know that I, in the beginning of 1990, together with my entire family, was a supporter of the ecological movement of the Greens in Sarajevo? If you don't know, never mind.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I -- I know that you were for a brief period of time at least a supporter of the Green movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was one of the leaders, and I chaired meetings, and I thought that that was the only thing that was worth working for and that's why I was there. All right. Mr. Donia, do you agree that on the 27th of March, a group of top Muslims disclosed that they would establish the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What year are we talking about? Doctor do you know the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 27th of March, 1990, this was made public; namely, an initiating committee was established. Do you know the names of the signatories? There were about 40 of them.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that among them there was Alija Izetbegovic, Omer Behmen, Hasan Cengic, and others, who later became the leadership of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were among them, yes. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the core of this group that was -- that established the SDA were people who were actually tried because of subversive political activity against the state in 1977 and in 1980?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there were a few people in this group, including Izetbegovic, Behmen, and I believe Cengic, who were prosecuted in 1947. I think the translation came across as 1977, but they were prosecuted in 1947, and Izetbegovic again was prosecuted by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, convicted, and imprisoned in 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Izetbegovic was among the founders and top officials of the organisation of the Young Muslims, starting from 1939.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this organisation was actually an affiliate of the well-known Muslim organisation of the Muslim Brethren from Egypt?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the organisation that assassinated Sadat because he was involved in peace talks with Israel. Have you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't think there's a link of any consequence between the Young Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the period of the, you know, immediate post World War II era and the Young Muslims of Egypt -- I'm sorry, the -- yes, the Muslim Brotherhood of Egypt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you heard of the great Jerusalem mufti el-Husseini who is the uncle or some similar relative of Yasser Arafat's?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've written in my Sarajevo book, in fact, about his -- about the mufti of Jerusalem, his visit to Bosnia during the Second World War, and his relationship to the Ustasha regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you know that he was a personal friend and ally of Hitler?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Hitler had personal friends. He was, as I say -- he had good relations with the Ustasha regime and certainly with the Berlin leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's from Hitler's point of view. Perhaps he didn't have any friends, but el-Husseini considered they were friends, and we saw a photograph of them together here, but do you agree that the el-Husseini visit to Bosnia-Herzegovina resulted in the creation of one and then another SS division, the Handzar Division. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and again I've written about that in my Sarajevo book and also the second book that I wrote with John Fine, "Bosnia-Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed." It's common knowledge, I would say, in the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, but the Trial Chamber is not aware of that. So the Chamber has to learn of these things. Now -- now, do you know where el-Husseini stayed when he was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that he stayed with Omer Behmen and he socialised with Alija Izetbegovic, would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you denying it then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But are you denying it? Do you say that that was not the case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was the case. I just simply said I do not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Because you don't know that's how it was, or because you know that that is not how it was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't know whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have 1D33, please. On e-court. 1D33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't seem to have the translation. I had hoped that we did, but I'll read it out. This is a prisoner's list for Alija Izetbegovic. The date is 1947. Name, surname, et cetera. Army military court found him guilty of acts against the nation and the state, and in 1976 that sentence was struck from the list because he'd served his sentence in actual fact. Now may we see page 35. But let me ask you first. Well, you said that you knew that he was sentenced to a prison term, but he was sentenced by the army court, right, for acts against the state and nation; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would concur with this document as evidence of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you think that that reference should have found a place in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. It did find a place in my book on Sarajevo, as I know, and I think I also mention it in the "Tradition Betrayed," book, but I think it was outside the purview, both chronologically and topically, of my Sarajevo report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but can we mark it for identification pending translation. I think some kind of failure in the LiveNote. I think it's a convenient time for a break after assigning the number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask -- [Interpretation] may I ask for 1D165, please, on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Dr. Donia. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know his father's name, Halid Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no. I believe that's accurate, but I didn't before you just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to the next page, please. It's an interview given by Halid Cengic speaking of his son Hasan. So next page, please. We haven't got a translation, I'll read it: "Halid Cengic, the main war logistics person of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an army and a Hadzija." May we turn to the next page, please. May we turn to the next page. What it describes on this page, actually, is how he was received by Dobrica Cosic and Ljubo Tadic and expressed their sympathy. Anyway, here it says Hasan, referring to his son: "Hasan left prison on November 1987, Alija, a year later. So in 1988. The SDA was created on the 26th of May, 1990. And on the -- we had the "Obznana." I think it was the 27th but it says 7th. "Until Alija and Omer had left prison, there was no mention of the party. What was most important for us at that point was for people to get out of prison. When Alija was released, circles began to peak -- speak about a party in Sarajevo, but the matter was also discussed out of the country." Did you know that the SDA party, the idea about a party, the nucleus of it, was within the circle of these prisoners doing sentence in prison?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- this -- this statement is correct that it wasn't until Izetbegovic was released from prison that this gathering took place that you mentioned in -- in February, and indeed the -- Izetbegovic's release was critical for the -- this nucleus of people to come together and make plans to form the Party of Democratic Action on the 26th of May, which I would point out is a different date than you used earlier, which was the February date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it was announced in March but formed on the 26th of May. I agree with that. May we turn to the next page please. In the highlighted area it says: "Foca was the centre for arming. It was from there that several thousand barrels were distributed all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Ljubinje to Srebrenica. Even Naser Oric came to collect arms there." Now, do you agree that Ljubinje was a predominantly Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the percentage of the populations and the peoples in Ljubinje was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it's 80 per cent, but we'll come to that. Anyway, Cengic goes on to say: "I don't know whether it was the centre or not, but we did assist various municipalities in BiH to the best of our ability." Now, since you speak Serbian, I'm sure you can read this and follow what I'm saying. And when the weapons were brought into Foca, nobody was to know about it let alone to take it into their homes. Saja, Sahinpasic complained to me and I said drive it to my house, and that's what happened. So the problem wasn't in the weapons, it was in the consciousness of the people and in the organisation. Now, did you know that Foca was armed in that way and that it was, in fact, a logistics centre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I don't think that's what this says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what he says. I don't know whether it was the centre, but we helped many other municipalities. So the weapons went from Foca to other municipalities. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when the weapons were brought to Foca, nobody was to know about it. Nor to take it into their homes. That's to me what it says. I don't know about the idea that it was a logistics centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it says here, I don't know whether it was a centre in actual fact, but we assisted. And when the weapons were taken to Foca, nobody dared take them over. So they had the problem of storing it. Not weapons. There were enough weapons, but the problem was who dared take the weapons home?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you yourself have now agreed that this states that it may not have been a centre at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report did you include this piece about arming and weapons in Foca?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to the next page now, please. The underlined part it says: "Precisely at the time of the meeting in Karadjordjevo, for 50 days he waited with people in Zagreb." It's Sahinpasic that he refers to as he. "And with the help of --" let's start from the beginning. "Saja, with the beginning of some people from Focatrans, took people, procured weapons, drove them in along with thousands of problems. During the time the meeting in Karadjordjevo, he waited for 50 days in Zagreb for the shipment because Gojko Susak promised him 5.000 pieces of weapons, barrels." Do you know who Gojko Susak was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I've not followed you on the rest of this article. I take it you're representing that this is a continuation of the same article?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same article, and I'm reading from the top part where it says Sahinpasic, nicknamed Saja, with the help of some people from Focatrans, the Focatrans company - and we'll come back to that in due course - procured weapons and that he waited in Zagreb because Gojko Susak promised him 5.000 barrels. Now, who was Gojko Susak?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not see Sahinpasic here. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Saja, nicknamed Saja. There you are.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saja. Okay. You've been saying Sahinpasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, to make it easier for you to understand. Saja is Senad Sahinpasic, a well known deputy from Foca. Now, who was Gojko Susak? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Susak was the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia after Tudjman's election as president in April of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we turn to the next page now, please. Do you know that a major crisis broke out in the Focatrans company before the elections while the Communists were still in power in Foca and that the Serbs were expelled from the Focatrans Company? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a major controversy erupting in Foca associated with Focatrans. I've never been able to figure out exactly what took place to set that off or -- I think it probably was never resolved fully, but I'm not actually -- I'm not actually familiar with the specifics of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here in this rectangle the question is: "You formed the first unit of Patriotic League and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And Cengic's answer is this: "Already on the 1st of August, 1990, during the defence of Focatrans, we had a platoon of arm -- a platoon armed with automatic weapons, a machine-gun, and a mortar. All of them had camouflage uniforms, and they took the oath in the Ustikolina mosque by placing their hand on the Koran. The unit was commanded by the late," "rahmetli" meaning "the late," "Husein Cavrk, major of the BH Army and holder of the golden lily. He was killed at Preluca near Gorazde. Kemo Karisik carried out a review of the unit and it was already a company at the time in September 1991." Now, can we see from this that on the 1st of August, 1990, that is to say, before the elections while the communists were still in power, that in Focatrans the first unit of the Patriotic League was formed and it was armed with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The reference to the Patriotic League, I believe, is in the question, not in the statement by Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But was an armed formation established that took the oath in a mosque with their hands on the Koran and that it was armed with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Cengic's assertion, and I believe that his words are represented accurately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now do you see that this man Kemo Karisik carried out a review of the company in September 1991, which is before the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslims made an airport in Visoko and -- constructed an airport in Visoko near Sarajevo? During the war that is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now move on two pages. Thank you. This is what it says on the right: "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1992, took the decision to construct an airport in a locality near Visoko." Now, the question is this: Did a plane ever land at that airport? And Cengic's answer is: "What our enemies know is something that our people should know too. Had we not had that airport, it would have been difficult for us," and then he uses this word "predeverati." I assume you know what that means. "We would have found it difficult to contend with the situation. Omer Kulic landed first on the 19th of April, 1994, when we had nothing. It -- had the Serbs known that they could have just walked in." And then he goes on to write that in 1995 already other special planes began landing bringing in other materiel and technical equipment. Do you believe Mr. Cengic? Do you believe that the airport existed in Visoko and that there were flights and landings carrying military equipment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Noting that this is quite late in the war, his first reference is to April of 1994, yeah, I find that plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, but just to ensure my understanding is correct, I take it when this Court has been marking documents for identification pending translation that refers to a translation of the document in its entirety rather than only these highlighted and circled portions. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D246, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D91 next, please. 1D91, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order on the appointment of Halid Cengic, the person we mentioned a moment ago, to see that he was well placed to talk about the matters he talked about. May we scroll down. Halid Cengic is appointed to the post of assistant commander for the reception, control, and distribution of materiel and also deputy commander of the centre in the organ for the reception, control, and distribution of material resources, and the rank is colonel brigadier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Stop there. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I believe there is a translation, a Defence translation, of this document, and it might be helpful for us all if both could be displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, this could be one and the same document as D00074.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's his son, Hasan Cengic, and that one was far more active, as we will see. Can we see the translation of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm always happy to be corrected if I've misrepresented something, Your Honour, but the document that we have as being released was the appointment of Hasan Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll move on with this untranslated document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Donia, do you see that Halid Cengic was appointed to this position and that what he said in that interview was well-founded? He deserved this position of a colonel or a brigadier in logistics in the Muslim army, although he hadn't held any rank before that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you've extrapolated too much from this document. This document simply says that he was appointed to this position. It doesn't really speak to his qualifications, his prior experience, or position in the organisation. It's just merely a notice of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But how is it that a man who is not a military officer can be appointed to such a high-ranking position? I am linking this to what we saw in the interview, that from 1990 onwards, he was arming the people of Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's not that unusual to see people in certain types of positions be given relatively high ranks in military organisations to exercise their particular professional expertise. So I wouldn't -- I'd say that is unremarkable. I don't see anything here about his background that would lead me to be concerned or to find it worthy of note that he was appointed to this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take into account at all his activity? I mean, in your report his activity in terms of arming the Muslims from the 1st of August, 1990, onwards?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've noted as a matter of general policy the formation of the Patriotic League in, I think, March of 1991. I have not specifically dealt with Halid Cengic or the arming of anyone at the local municipal level largely because it's just simply outside the purview of my -- my commission to prepare the report. It's interesting though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And before that, are you trying to say that the OTP asked you not to take into account the arming of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's evident by the fact that I addressed it in the report. What I'm saying is that the OTP and I came together on an agreement that I would deal with specific topics dealing with the -- the SDS Bosnian Serb leadership. One could, I am sure, write an entire treatise on the activities of these sort of Muslim politicians in waiting in the very late days of socialism, but that was a bit outside of my -- my brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can the actions of the Serbs be understood even if one does not present what it was that led to those actions? You said yourself the other day during the direct examination that it is a historian's job to establish the link between cause and consequence. Can the position of the Serbs be understood at all if we do not shed more light on the circumstances in which they operated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the purpose of our -- the endeavour is to understand the position of the Serbs and the circumstances in which they operated, and I personally don't attribute much importance to this Focatrans incident in terms of spinning up the actions of the SDS in the subsequent period, but it's certainly a factor in the environment generally in which people were operating. The -- this was one of a couple of local incidents that took place that kind of sort of roiled the environment in the period from 87 to 90. I don't think that any of those things predetermined actions or mandated a particular course of action by the SDS after it was formed in July of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you said that Serbs would often say that they do something and then we do something. That is what you said. Wouldn't it be useful if you portrayed certain actions the way you did on the basis of what you actually said yourself, and you quoted me? Wouldn't it be necessary to shed more light on the preceding action taken by the Muslim police and that caused a reaction on the part of the Serbs? Can we see the truth at all if we do not look at it that way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say this, you did, and you also, for example, said that you deliberately waited to form the SDS until the Croat and Muslim parties were organised so that the SDS could never be accused of fomenting inter-ethnic rivalry. These are your statements. I did not task myself to identify specifically what happened and how you reacted to it. I think one could do that for the events that I spoke of yesterday from October 1991 to April of 1992. I think it's a little bit more difficult to do that prior to the October -- October 15 events. But one could look at the whole scope of activities and see these things. I would not want to attribute a linear causation to these actions. I think there was a period of time certainly in which there was -- there were a lot of options to be taken by everybody concerned, and -- so wouldn't get as specific as I guess you'd like to hear in attributing event A to event B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Serb dissidents and intellectuals on the 28th of June, 1990, renewed the Prosvjeta Serb cultural society that had been banned sometime after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Concurrent with the revival of the cultural societies of other groups, yes. This all happened right about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that Serbian elite had opted for not establishing a political party? Rather, they wanted to meet all the needs of the Serb people through this Prosvjeta society.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that's not true. I think by your own account in some published statements there was considerable agitation to form a Serbian national party starting at the very beginning of 1990. The first efforts went to try to form a branch of a party in a neighbouring republic. First of all, the democratic party with Mr. Cavoski and a few other people. And then there were some efforts to form a party that was going to be a branch of the SDS in Croatia, and that initiative was put down by some people who were advising you at that time, including Mr. Cosic, who suggested to you that it would be better to have a party that was not an affiliate of any party in a neighbouring republic. And so I think that your own position, which was that you were very interested in seeing a party formed but you were not willing or prepared at that point to assume the leadership of the party, attests to the fact that you were there was a lot going on to organise and create a party. Mr. Vladimir Srebrov talked about -- or, actually, I think announced the formation of a Serb national party in Drvar in February, and so there was a lot going on to move toward the direction -- toward forming a political party at that time. By the time that Prosvjeta was created there were people in the group, certainly in this group of the elite or as you call them the leading intellectuals, who wanted to do things strictly through Prosvjeta but that was not the only thing that was going on and indeed the party went on to organise very shortly after that and to have its formal founding on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you agree that it was established quite late, about four months prior to the elections, and that didn't really leave much time to get properly organised; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the establishment of parties actually proceeded all at about the same time. The first party to hold its founding Assembly was actually the Social Democratic Party League of Communists on May 25th. The second party to organise formally was the Party of Democratic Action on May 26th. You were third on July 12th. The fourth party to organise, major party to organise, was the Reformists. That was on July 27. And the final party to organise formally was the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Community, and that was on August 18th. So in line here I see the SDS organising third and two parties had even less time by that metric to prepare for the election than the rest of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the HDZ was active in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Western Herzegovina, considerably before it was actually established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that all the major national parties -- all the parties, for that matter, with the possible exception of the Reformists, were active in Bosnia-Herzegovina considerably before they were formally established, and, in fact, were caught in somewhat of a dilemma because of the law passed in February 1990 that approved the formation of political parties but not along national or religious lines. And so much of the activity that you're speaking of was actually carried out with the understanding that it was illegal, and the people who were doing it could be prosecuted. You made references to this yourself and indicated that you had many people organising on behalf of the SDS but operating illegally. The HDZ took a little bit different approach and operated pretty much in private gatherings, and the Party of Democratic Action, the Muslim party, took a different approach and adopted a nonnational name in its organising activities and believed in so doing it was in conformance with the law forbidding the organisation along national and religious lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us try to clear up a few matters. First of all, I claim that the Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not affiliate of the Serb Democratic Party from Croatia, rather, it took over the insignia and the programme of that party. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, do you agree that at municipal level we could establish a national party for a while but not at central level, and that is why in every municipality we established a separate party and later on they were all brought together, and that would perhaps speak about that illegality that you had referred to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding of that process was that there were some spontaneous local efforts to organise a Serb national party, a major one, in Eastern Herzegovina, one in the Drvar area. You referred to some organising efforts in Romanija, which would be the area around Sarajevo, and it was to prevent this from developing into a factionalised organisation, that you did indeed step up and seek to create a single centralised organisation and to bring these separate spontaneous groups or organising groups together. You then had the idea to form a party that had at least two wings. One was to be the national wing, which was led by you, and the other was the social democratic league wing which was to be led by -- I forget who it was. It was -- but this, I think, was -- you received -- according to your account, you received advice from Mr. Cosic that this was indeed a really bad idea, which I think it probably was, to form a party that built into it factions. And though you held to that idea in the period probably right up till September of 1990, it was something that you had to be dissuaded from doing by Mr. Cosic and other advisors to the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the main concern of the Serb intelligentsia was that the Serb people would have no one to vote for except for the formal Communists, just like the Serbs in Croatia voted for Racan's Communists, and that that was the motive for establishing the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's one of the motives. I do believe that the results of the Croatian elections, which were in late -- mid-April, came as something of a jolt to the Serb nationals -- nationalists, yourself and others, in Bosnia and probably stirred you to action because you looked at the prospect of the same thing happening, which was that most Serbs, in fact, voted for the League of Communists rather than the -- the Croatian SDS party. So, yes, I think that was a factor. I think there were -- there was a general evolving sense that there had to be a point of unification for Serb organising efforts in Bosnia, and the idea of having a separate party, as you say, taking the name and programme from -- not -- not -- let's say repeating them for a separate party in Bosnia was the best way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with Lord Owen that the Serbs in Croatia were frightened because World War II insignia and rhetoric had come back and that they had reason for their fear? They had reason to fear a return to 1941. That was actually the title of a book, "1941, Coming Back."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not familiar with the book. Who is the author?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a statement made by David Owen, and the book is authored by Goldstein, the president of the Jewish community in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the general statement that the Serbs in Croatia were frightened by the revival of World War II insignia and rhetoric emanating from not only the HDZ but other Croatian bodies. It -- I think one has to be careful about exactly when one would speak about that phenomenon, because there was a genuine effort to achieve an agreement that would resolve that concern in the summer of 1990, prior to the -- prior to the adoption of the constitution. So in -- as a general principle, I would agree that they had reason to be concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see this part that pertains to Lord Carrington, who chaired the peace conference. We will see him speaking about what you talked to us about just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The war saw it differently "The Serbs in Croatia and, indeed, outside Croatia had a very vivid memory of what happened in 1941, '42, when Hitler declared Croatia as an independent puppet state, if you like, and the horrors that went on there and the murders of the Serbs were still very -- I mean, a very large number of Serbs were murdered at that time. I mean, hundreds of thousands. And I think it was very understandable that when Croatia declared its independence and promulgated a new constitution without any safeguard for the 600.000 Serbs who still lived in Croatia, that the Croatian -- that the Serbs were very perturbed about this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with Lord Owen -- or, rather, Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully, no.
