And I point out you played one part of a, very, I think, controversial tape that gives a very one-sided view of not only the events in question but carefully selects excerpts from key policy-makers on their views. So I think -- I've agreed already that there was cause for concern in the wake of the promulgation of that constitution which it looks to me like was in part a product of the failure of the Serbs to -- of Serb representatives to offer the appropriate language that they were asking for. So in terms of the time that he's speaking of, I do agree with that. I think also you have to look at the progression of events which is much broader than what he attempts to deal with and conclude accordingly what the responsibility for that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now we're only dealing with the Serbs in Bosnia, whether they had any reason to worry about insignia and rhetoric, and now let us see whether they had cause for concern regarding the actions of the new government. Let us see what it was that the new government it did. Actually, did you include that in your own report, that the Serbs in Croatia had cause for concern?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave a fairly extensive account of the events. I wouldn't maybe say extensive, but I certainly covered the events in Croatia in my -- in one of my reports. So that -- that topic did, in fact, receive some attention. I don't know that I put it exactly the way you just formulated it, but was certainly prepared to note the phenomenon in my writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Lord Carrington says here that the proclamation of Croatia's independence without ensuring rights for 600.000 Serbs was a reason for great concern amongst the Serbs. That is what this is all about. Croatia declared its independence against the will and wishes of one of the constituent peoples of Croatia before this community had received any kind of guarantees. Was that included in your report, that the premature recognition of Croatia led to the catastrophe of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I did, in fact, cover the events associated with the -- or I gave an account of the events associated with the Croatian move to independence and the Serbian movement within Croatia for -- to form separate associations, to rally the population behind the separatist project. Again, I didn't formulate it the way that you just did and would not think that this is -- I don't agree with the way you put it. I think that one would have to take a more nuanced look at it and not conflate these events between the spring of 1990 and June 25th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way, Mr. Donia: Up until the arrival of Tudjman in power, were the Serbs a constituent peoples in Croatia? Was it the republic of Croats and Serbs? That's what its name was. Yes or no? We can deal with that quickly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that in the constitution of Croatia, in all the constitutions of the Republic of Croatia, the wording was always that Croatia was the republic of the Croats and Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you asked me about the name of the republic. I told you the name of the republic is the Republic of Croatia. I don't think you're contesting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Hello.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we lost just a little bit in the translation here and the dead microphone. We agree, I take it, that the name of the republic was the Republic of Croatia, that in the name there was no mention of Serbs. Was there a mention of Serbs in the constitution? Yes, and I believe we agree on that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So are they stipulated as being one of the two constituent peoples of Croatia, constituting Croatia as a state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the new authority, did it introduce new rhetoric or, rather, the old rhetoric of 1941? Did it re-introduce that rhetoric? We agreed, I think, that it did; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- look, there was some revival of those things, but I think that the official circles tried to avoid at least the most ostentatious of it, and I think it depended on who you're speaking about and the degree to which those symbols and that rhetoric was re-introduced. The -- the whole issue of translating this Stalinist notion of constituent nations, which came to really be just an article of faith, an unquestioned part of nationality policy in Yugoslavia, the whole issue of translating that into a democratic period was to me extremely fraught, and I'm just not certain that it -- that concept worked very well or works very well in a democratically elected system. So I'm perfectly happy to note these designations of the constituent peoples in the Communist people period, but I think that you really have to recognise that the movement to that to a different system caused all sorts of problems and challenges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know that there are national states and civilian states?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that simple. I think, you know, the -- what one would think of as the national states of Western Europe all have systems of government that are based on the civil concept, and I don't know that there is a pure case of a national state without some civil element, or -- and there are probably very few examples of a civil state with no national element.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know, that Slovenia wiped out tens of thousands of its citizens coming from the southern republics in origin from its register of civilians of Slovenia because they weren't Slovenes. Do you know about that? It erased them from the list.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which list -- no. The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know that President Tudjman said at an HDZ meeting that the Independent State of Croatia was not only a fascist creation but was also the realisation of the legitimate aspirations of the Croatian people for their state, for a state of their own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar that he said words to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that he also said that he was happy that his wife was neither a Serb nor a Jew?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that President Tudjman christened a Muslim family, an eight member Muslim family?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to play -- well, do you know this person that we're seeing now?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I know both the person on the left and the film you're about to play, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, who is it then? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Martin Spegelj who was -- I don't know exactly what his title was, but he was in the government of Croatia by late 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think you're right. He was the defence minister, in actual fact. May we now play this. It's the 19th of November, 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just before we get into another video, I note on the record the 65 ter number of that last video-clip was never uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was 1408. And in that regard, I also noted as the transcript was playing that on page 45, line 23, there seems to be a line missing in regard to Dr. Donia's observation as regards the video from which that clip was drawn. He said something -- my recollection is to the effect that it was a controversial film, and his -- so that line appears to be missing, and it's -- my notation is page 45, line 23, and his comments run to page 46, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be checked or that has been reinstated by your comment. Do you have, Mr. Karadzic, the 65 ter number of this video-clip that you're going to play now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says on the tape, I assume. At least I hope so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it reads 1D892.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 19th of October, 1990, and the Yugoslav People's Army knew about this. May we play the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, are we supposed to hear anything?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you should be hearing the Serbo-Croatian -- or, rather, Croatian, if that is a separate language, but the subtitles are in English, but, yes, we should hear the sound. So may we put the volume up and have some sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you expect the interpreters to read out these subtitles, or if they can, they can translate, interpret, what they hear on the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot interpret without a transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll play both, because the subtitles are a translation of what Martin Spegelj is actually saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I've just heard from the interpreters that they can't interpret without the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But we can read the subtitles, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's give it a try.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there's still no soundtrack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was just told that the soundtrack in B/C/S is very weak and they can't hear anything. Would you like them to read out the subtitles?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps that would be best, because the subtitles are the correct translation. But if you remember, I played this footage, this film, during my opening statement. There seems to be something wrong now. We'll try something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Donia, that Martin Spegelj was caught in this action where he's educating his killers on the ground and that at the time he had 80.000 Kalashnikovs, and that he was training them and telling them how JNA officers should be shot in the stomach?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I love this video. In fact, I start out one chapter in "Tradition Betrayed," speaking about it because it is -- it's a very dramatic moment that shows both, I think, the advanced point at which the Croatian Defence forces were contemplating and were preparing for conflict and also the degree to which the KOS, the counter-intelligence service of the JNA was intent on discrediting the Croatian leadership. KOS is something like the American FBI in that it monitors perceived threats against security to the state. So it's to me just a very vivid example of what was going on at the time and, in fact, was played at a session of the Federal Presidency or at least a session at which the -- which Tudjman was present in January of 1991, and in a sense worsened relations at that point between the presidents of the various republics because of the two things that it shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try and play it again. I hope it will be successful this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe we could try, Your Honour. I think it might be working from the machines on this side of the courtroom for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be just more proof of the inequality of arms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voice-over] There are 9.000 JNA officers and 18.000 JNA soldiers on the whole territory of Slovenia, Croatia, and part of Bosnia. We have now 80.000 people armed with Kalashnikovs. "We will resolve Knin in the way that we will butcher them. We have the international -- especially now when this whore has won in Serbia. We will butcher them. Milosevic? Yes. Now two days after he had won the Americans offered to help us. And up until then they had only speculated. They said now it will be like this: 1.000 armoured vehicles, cars, who knows what else. They will provide weapons and equipment for 100.000 soldiers, all free of charge. The army has no business there. They will be massacred. Everybody will be massacred already in their homes. To kill on the spot, on the street, in the army barracks compound, anywhere, just take a pistol and shoot in the stomach. This will not be a conventional war. "It will be a civil war with no consideration towards anyone. Not even towards women or children. The bombs simply need to be thrown into family apartments. Physical liquidation. Somebody enters the apartment. The courier. He appears in front of the door bang, bang, bang, and returns downstairs. Let them call the police to establish who it was. Then down the stairs he goes to the other and kills him at the same time. Don't mind the women or the children. It does not matter. "Boljkovac: We will use all means. We will also use weapons. Serbs will never again be in Croatia as long as we are here."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise the other man, Josip Boljkovac, the second man who appeared?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Donia, you describe this in your book, but did you include it in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the filming of this footage in the Presidency deteriorated the relationship between the presidents in the republic -- or, I mean the members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume Mr. Milosevic didn't appreciate being called a whore, and certainly was evidence of a high-ranking Croatian official plotting against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did the filming deteriorate relations or the actual fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both, but the -- the evidence in the film would be -- was the primary contributor to the deterioration of relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it say there that they would massacre the Serbs in Knin? And Boljkovac adds that the Serbs will never be what they had previously been in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we've seen what it says, and I don't know that I want to take a paraphrase other than the text of what actually has been entered into the record. So I think it says what it says. It's clear that that's the -- that's a nasty piece of intent, to massacre people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that that had to give rise to the Serbs' concern in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. This really pertained to Croatia and might have been -- might have contributed to, let's say, fear on the part of some Serbs in Bosnia, but I think in general the feeling was that by Bosnians in general that what was going on in Croatia was something different than what was going on in Bosnia. This is, after all, the time, January of 1991, when you formed a government with the HDZ, and the SDA designated the ministers that you wanted to designate and prepared or initiated this period of a partnership amongst the three national parties. So I would have to say, I think, that this is something that probably had much more impact in Croatia than in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me now remind you of the 26th of May, 1990, the founding Assembly of the SDA party. Do you remember that at that founding SDA party session, Dalibor Brozovic, a high-ranking official, Croatian, said that Croatia would defend itself along the Drina River, alluding to the fact that Croatia -- or, rather, that Bosnia was part of the Independent State of Croatia, or had been part of the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, just to note that Mr. Brozovic was not -- he was there as a guest of the -- of the SDA. He was not a part of the organising function of that founding Assembly. I don't recall him saying -- referring to the NDH, but he did indeed say that Croatia would consider the boundary -- its boundary to be the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that another party, the Croatian Party of Rights, said that Croatia would be established within the boundaries that the Independent State of Croatia once had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 26th of May, 1990, was I in politics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time you were very politically engaged in talks and meetings and arrangements for what was going to follow in very short order. I don't think you held any formal position in -- in political life until the 12th of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, on the 3rd of July, in a talk show on television, it was announced that there would be such a party, but on the 26th of May we still didn't know that there would be a Serbian Democratic Party. There was no talk of that yet. Can you remember a single public event, or secret event for that kind, of the Serbian Democratic Party or speech or intellectual circle on the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, no. I'd have to check records to see if that was the case, but I think in terms of your own account and the account of some of your closest friends and observers, activity that eventually led to the formation of the SDS was going on very early in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this video into evidence now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous one as well, Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it he refers to the excerpts that were played in court and to that I would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We understand that a transcript will be submitted in due course?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as soon as we get it, we will provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we shall mark for identification until that time both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 1D1408 will be MFI D248, and 65 ter 1D892 will be MFI D249.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just again, those 65 ter numbers refer to the whole videos which -- the first one of which is extremely long, so I take it we're just referring to the clips that were played in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I should have noted the time-frame, but I couldn't note it. So I'll leave it to the court Defence team to identify exactly what portion was played in the courtroom. Yes, we have more -- is it convenient to take a break now? Yes. We will have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us finish with Croatia before the outbreak of the war. Mr. Donia, let me read the actual wording from the constitution before this last one, namely that Croatia is the state of the Croatian and Serbian peoples as well as others living in it. And the new constitution says: "The Republic of Croatia is being established as the national state of the Croatian people." And the state of members of autonomous minorities, Serbs, Czechs, Hungarians, Germans, Jews, et cetera. So now instead of being a constituent people the Serbs were turned into a national minority. That is why we had to see how it was that Yugoslavia came into being. Also the fact that the Serbs had united with Serbia as a state-forming people to the west of the Drina. In Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, actually, do you know that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state of equal peoples and citizens, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and members of other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several different questions there. I don't see a document that you actually were reading from. If you could just identify what exactly you're reading from. You were reading from the constitution of the Republic of Croatia? From what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first one was the pre-Tudjman constitution and the other one, that it was the state of the Croatian people and national minorities, including Serbs, that is the Tudjman's Christmas constitution, the so-called Christmas constitution of the 22nd of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1990. Okay. Okay. Thank you. Now, your next question was about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I don't believe you quite read that constitutional provision in full. I don't know if you have a document that would provide that or it's a fairly delicately worded provision, and it changed, I believe, in July of 1990, if I'm not mistaken, with the adoption of amendment 60. So I just would want to be clear on exactly what you're reading from and what date it was enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from my notes. So what I copied here was the wording concerning the Republic of Croatia before Tudjman and after Tudjman. Just from the point of view of the constitutionality of the Serbs. That's what I'm talking about. Now, as far as the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, Article 1 says that: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of equal citizens and peoples, Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and members of other peoples and nationalities living there." Article 2: "Bosnia-Herzegovina is within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I was just interested in the following: What happened in Croatia? Were the Serbs thrown out of the constituent peoples and thrown into the national minorities? And what happened in Bosnia? Did they remain as one of the peoples?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one by one. Doctor, you wanted to comment upon his question about Croatian constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've given that, made that comment. I concur with the reading that he did of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So -- well, unlike in Croatia where the constitutional -- or new constitution was adopted in December, and it was discussed for some months before then, the Bosnian constitution underwent changes in July of 1990 that were approved by the outgoing Communist-dominated Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the version that you just read was, I believe, the version of Article 1 that resulted from those changes. So, yes, that's -- that's the way things stood as at the end of July 1990. And I believe, furthermore, if you go to the other -- there are several articles in the first part of the constitution which not only mention these three peoples, but they actually change the order so that one of the peoples is first in amendment 1, another is first in one of the subsequent amendments, and -- and then they switch it yet to the third. So I would have to say there was a great deal of attention to this -- the relative -- to the equality of these peoples in the constitution of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You do agree that in paragraph 2, Article 1, it says that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything in front of me to that effect, but I certainly don't contest it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Serb Democratic Party -- or, rather, Professor Koljevic and I, had asked the Assembly to introduce a Chamber of Nations in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on that very same July, before the amendments were passed, to have a Chamber of Nations within the Assembly. Actually, respond to that first. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that all three national parties in Bosnia appealed in the -- this organising period of organising the parties for the inclusion of a Chamber of Nation -- a Chamber of Nations, yes. I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that amendment 70, paragraph 10 to the constitution on the 31st of July, 1990, envisaged the establishment of a council for looking into matters pertaining to the equality of rights of peoples within Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That was actually instead of having a proper Chamber of Nations. That was the only concession they were willing to make. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, there's a very good succinct description of this very situation in -- I think it's the first entry of my Excerpts report, by Mr. Krajisnik from -- I believe it's the first Bosnian Serb Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the SDA never allowed this council to be established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my -- I don't think that's my understanding of it, and it's not exactly Mr. Krajisnik's understanding of it either. The dispute was not about its establishment. It was about what its jurisdiction was going to be, and failure to reach an agreement on that meant that it was never created.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what was envisaged was for this council to operate on the principles of consensus and that 20 MPs would have the right to send a particular issue to the council and the question would remain pending in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D01391. Could we have that, please. And in the meantime, Mr. Donia, do you remember that the first attempt to pass a declaration on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been halted because the Assembly, including the SDA, had accepted the fact that this question had to be dealt with by the council for the equality of national rights first? That was in the spring of 1991; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're very close. The SDA submitted a proposal which was characterized as declaration of sovereignty that included essentially new language about this, proclaiming the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I forget how many points, four or five or six points. And as that was about to come to a vote, the members of the SDS appealed to the parliamentarian for a ruling. That was Mr. Campara. And, in fact, he ruled that the resolution had to be referred to the council that we're talking about, the substitute for the separate Chamber, before it could be voted on. Since there was no such council in effect or in existence, the legislation died at that point. And indeed the parties did accept that, and it fell off the agenda of the Assembly, not to come back until the fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you know our language, in all fairness this is Cyrillic, but this is the Serb Democratic Party, the Main Committee, and do you see here it says number and date? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if we look at 65 ter number 17566, we'll see another version of that document that's been translated into English. And I hope I've not misled you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that this time that you are absolutely correct. Let's try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the number and the date underneath the heading where it says "Main Board"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the number 01-79/90, and the date of 8 October 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that all the documents that had gone through party organs bear a number and a date?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not been my experience that all of them do, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then those were documents that had not gone through party organs. Well, let's have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic, can you confirm the document you are seeing is the exact identical document you're referring to? I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a translation of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So actually, we're not going to look at the entire document, but let us see what the party is asking for. Amendment 17 [as interpreted] is not in accordance with amendment 60. Amendment 17 [as interpreted] reads: "The Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state of citizens with equal rights and peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats as well as members of other nations and nationalities living in Bosnia-Herzegovina." "Amendment 70, section 1 does not provide for the national equality of Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim nationalities, and it is not in accordance with amendment 60, and it does not allow for amendment 60 to be put into practice." "The Serb Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina demands that amendment 70 conform with amendment 60 and that section 10 of this amendment be amended and that section 10 of amendment 70 be extended to include the following text: "At the request of no less than 20 deputies in the Council of Citizens and Council of Municipalities in respect of issues relevant for the fulfillment of the principle of national equality and, in particular," and now the six questions are specified. "The Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall establish the following three national councils: The Serbian National Council, the Muslim National Council, and the Croatian National Council which will be composed of all deputies from both Assembly councils, the issues of interest for the realisation of the national equality in the Assembly of the SRBH shall be decided in accordance with a separate procedure. "Decisions shall be considered adopted if a simple majority of deputies in each of the three national councils vote in favour." So do you see that we ask for the consistent implementation of the constitution through all the amendments involved and that could have saved us from a great deal of trouble?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is when I'm glad I'm not a constitutional scholar, because separating out which amendment should prevail in two constitutional amendments numbered 60 and 70 is far beyond my ability to -- to do. I would note that the document prescribes -- I look at it kind of as a historian as an effort to ratchet up or elevate the role of the parties, the national parties, to equate them to the national communities and to kind of put the parties in a position to veto legislation on behalf of national communities using this device of the concepts inherent in -- in amendment 70 -- or I'm sorry, amendment 60. I don't see the rest of the document. I just see the first page, but that would be my comment on this. I guess it was a proposal that in the form this read was -- stood no chance of being accepted by the other -- other two national parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say parties here anywhere? It says here consisting proportionately of all political parties. That goes without saying. But there is no reference to political parties, rather, ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbian Democratic Party of BH demands that amendment 70 conform with amendment 60." I think that's a reference to a party, and pretty clearly an effort to elevate the party's status to essentially acquire the right to represent the national community in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that there is some misunderstanding here, Mr. Donia. The party is not asking that for themselves but for the ethnic community. One set of elections is won by one party and another set of elections can be won by another party, so this so has to do with the proportionality of all political parties. Does it say here that this has to do with political parties or is it the National Council?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment was that this is -- this is a time when you and leaders of other parties are desperately trying to establish the fact that you embodied the -- the will of the Serb people and the Serb national community and that the SDS embodied that will and interest. So this to me is something that attempts to further extend that claim to be the embodiment of the will of the -- of the Serb people with this demand. I still can't see the second page. I don't know what this goes on to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 2 in English, and in Serbian too. I mean, both in Serbian and in English. While we're waiting for that, Mr. Donia, do you agree that 31 point something per cent were Serbs and that the SDS won 97 per cent of all Serb votes because they won about 90 -- 31 per cent of all votes; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're, I think, referencing a couple of different things here. Are you referring to the census and -- the 1991 census and the per cent of the total population who declared themselves as Serbs in the census, or are you talking about the election outcome?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm comparing these two proportions, as it were. About 32 per cent of the population of Bosnia were Serbs, and we won about 31 per cent of the vote. So I'm saying that most Serbs voted for the Serb Democratic Party; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that most Serbs voted for the Serb Democratic Party. I don't think that percentage is right, because a good number of Serbs also voted for the non-national parties, the Social Democrats, and the Reformists. And, in fact, you complained about that a great deal in the period after the election and viewed it as your job to make sure that they saw the error of their ways and came to the -- rallied to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serb Democratic Party won 72 seats in parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Out of, I believe, 240, if I'm not mistaken. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there was a total of 86 Serbs in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that 83 of the 86 had established the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to this day the Assembly of Republika Srpska has 83 MPs; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. That's interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the Serb Democratic Party had 72. Then there was one from the Serb Renewal Movement, and the rest were among the Reformists, Socialists, et cetera. Out of those 86, 83 were against the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they moved to the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's approximately correct. I can't confirm for you that specific number, but in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will agree that 83 is more than one-third and that these MPs, even on the assumption that all the Muslims and Croats had wanted secession, that these 83 could nevertheless prevent the Assembly from Bosnia -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina from declaring independence; right? Because two-third -- a two-third majority is required for constitutional decisions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a number of assumptions built into that proposition that I'm not sure are right. I don't believe that the -- I don't know that it came to a vote in terms of what the actual number of votes against the independence would be in the Assembly. Of course, the probably more decisive factor was the referendum held in late February and 1st of March, 1992, which you and the SDS boycotted. And furthermore, you walked out of the Assembly. So I don't know that that would be -- that you can jump to the -- leap to the conclusion that 6 -- 83 people would have voted against independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm going to read this out to you. "Amendment 42, paragraph 1, bullet point 2: "The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina: "Borders of the republic can be changed by a decision of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina only provided that the will of all the citizens of the republic is expressed by way of a referendum if at least two-thirds of the total number of voters vote in favour of that." So the referendum towards the end of February 1992, did two-thirds of the total number of voters vote in favour of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'd like to you show me the document if you could that says this. I'm kind of stuck here just following your words and the translation of your words. I'd sure prefer to be looking at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree on the whole that in any country a simple majority would not be sufficient for carrying out constitutional changes, but more than that would be required?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say in most countries that's -- that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to play another little video-clip, and let's hear what Lord Carrington has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "This was a war that European leaders believe could have been avoided. "The Bosnian Serbs until comparatively recently have been in the majority in Bosnia, and then the Muslims who had had a very much higher birth rate than the Serbs became the predominant -- the majority population, and this of course was something very hard for the Serbs to swallow, and they made it abundantly plain very early on that they were not prepared to accept the situation in which there was an independent Bosnia under the constitution which then prevailed. And indeed under the constitution which then prevailed, it was illegal for Izetbegovic to declare independence because any constitutional change of that magnitude had to be agreed by all three parties."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to put this to you, Mr. Donia: What I read out was from the constitution, but I can't find the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I assume that all the constitutions exist. But anyway, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not provide for the independence and existence of Bosnia outside Yugoslavia at all. Do you agree? Is there any provision of the constitution saying that Bosnia can secede?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you think -- well, how can you not know? You must know something like that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a constitutional expert, and I'm certainly not a constitutional expert on the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I say, I would not want to be one and have to sort out these apparently directly conflicting positions of various amendments to the constitution. And I think that -- exists for the question of the republic becoming independent as well, differing things stated in different articles that would come in to play in that decision, and I can't sort them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the previous document into evidence and then move on. And the video extract, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Assembly session transcript is the minute. 17566 will be admitted as ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that video-clip. Do you have an objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, and it seems like it's another clip from 1D01408, which Dr. Donia already referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so. And then I -- for the record, I note that the clip ran from 47 minutes, 20 seconds, to 48 minutes, 06 seconds. So that part of the video-clip will be marked for identification till we receive the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we heard the number. It's MFI Exhibit D251.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 251, that's MFI D251.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in your report, Mr. Donia, did you make any mention at all of questions of a constitutional nature? You mentioned boundaries and municipalities. Is that not a constitutional question as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- it could be, and I think in part it is, but it's also matter of political decisions, which is the -- let's say the spirit in which I addressed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that somebody has the right to make political decisions having to do with constitutional matter in an unconstitutional way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. If one has the ability to determine what is constitutional and what is unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, common sense would allow you to make that determination. Now, Mr. Donia, I'm going to put something to you now, and here it is: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not provide for the possibility of secession from Yugoslavia just as the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me respond to your comment first that common sense would allow to you make that determination. I think the point of my answer here is to say no, it doesn't. It is a matter of constitutional interpretation that allows you to make that determination, and what I find was that all parties at this time to this conflict were freely throwing around the allegation that the other side was engaging in unconstitutional behaviour. It became a litany of complaints. For example, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina called unconstitutional the mobilisation of soldiers in Bosnia for the war in Croatia that was carried out on -- at the very end of September 1991, and they cited five different ways in which what was going on was unconstitutional. They never bothered to consult the Constitutional Court or to even ask for a ruling on the constitutionality of what they were doing. They simply declared it. And I think you were essentially doing the same thing at this time, and now you're trying to do it with me. I can't make that determination. I would argue that all of you who were throwing this terminology around at the time consistently refrained from submitting these arguments to a constitutional court and chose instead to just fight them out on the basis of denouncing the other side for acting that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that federal matters should be resolved by the federal constitution; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- in most cases I believe that's the case, but I'm not sure it's always true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the federal constitution in Yugoslavia proclaimed several decisions of the secessionist republics as unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the federal constitution didn't declare them unlawful, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The federal Constitutional Court proclaimed some decisions taken by the republics as being unlawful because they delved into the composition of the constitution and they were deemed unlawful.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out now what it says in article 5 of the federal constitution, and that relates to common reason: "The territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is one and is made up of the territories of the socialist republics." And one of the following articles says that the borders of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia cannot be changed without agreement from all the republics and autonomous provinces. Now, is it common sense that there can be no secession until everybody agrees about secession?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hate to repeat the point, but this is not a common-sense question. It is one assertion of this principle that, in fact, had other formulations that were in at least some potential conflict with it. So I can't make the judgement based on the question that you just asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider that the secession of those reports, the ones which did secede, did you consider that to be legal, lawful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't make judgements like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may we have 1D163 called up next on e-court, please. And while we're the waiting for that, Mr. Donia, if you are unable to say, then how can you assess the conduct and steps taken by the Serb side engulfed by this mass of unlawful conduct and moves on the other side, because you've been evaluating all our steps and movements, the municipal boundaries, resistance to the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth, and we say that it was all a result of the unlawful action of the Bosnian Croatian coalition in the Assembly. Now, let's see what Antonio Cassese says about this, a professor of law and a Judge of this Tribunal and President of the Tribunal at one time. Next page, please. The highlighted portion. "[In English] The achievement of independence by Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia can therefore be seen as a revolutionary process that has taken place beyond the regulation of the existing body of laws." [Interpretation] Do you accept that? Do you accept that Mr. Antonio Cassese is an expert in the field?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will certainly more than concede his status an expert in the field. I would also suggest you read the next paragraph which indeed suggests that the -- there is some qualifications to what he said about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the referendums, Mr. Donia, must go back to the Assemblies, and the deputies must reach a decision. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think you're just proving the point that the legal constitutional system with its multilayers and many, often conflicting, provisions just provides a great deal of fodder for those who would declare one part -- one act or another of their rivals to be unconstitutional. I -- it certainly, you know, was the case that referendums resulted in Assembly resolutions. I don't know whether they were considered binding or not, just as I really don't know whether these rulings by the Constitutional Court were considered binding or whether they were, in fact, also referred to Assemblies for further action. So I just don't know how to respond to your question. I can't answer your question yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the previous paragraph which talks about the right to self-determination. "[In English] ... adopted by the committee of the Yugoslav Federal Assembly on January the 20th, 1992, was never passed by the Plenary Assembly because it was rapidly overtaken by the dramatic secession of various republics." [Interpretation] Do you know that there was preparation for a law, a legal basis -- or, rather, ways and means for the republics to secede should they wish to do so, but the secessionist republics avoided and bypassed that and opted for the war option?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I didn't know about this proposed or draft law. I would not accept your characterization of the republics opting for the war option. I think that the road to war in both Slovenia and Croatia was more complicated than that and not -- not a simple matter of one -- one side opting for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know a statement made by President Tudjman who said that there would have never been a war had Croatia not wanted war, and that war provided us with independence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what his statement was. He at one point said words approximately to that effect. Again, I don't see any document that would say exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask how the opinion of a scholar or -- is relevant? You can use it in your submission later on, but I don't understand how it can become evidence before this Chamber. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the relevancy of a scholar, Judge Cassese, is more relevant than newspaper articles that we accepted and were commented on by Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was not there at the time. We will not admit this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we then have 1D163 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of Mr. Tudjman's words, and he uttered them at a large rally. He said there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted war. We'll show that and present it to you. He said there wouldn't have been a war had Croatia not wanted it. And Izetbegovic said, "We could have opted for peace but then we would have had to stay in Yugoslavia, and we opted for war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have the number right? Was Cassese article not 1D163?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 162. 162. There seems to be some mistake. 1D162. Yes, it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were statements made by the these two men, two presidents, the president of Croatia and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they opted for the war option?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to see the document if you could be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this will be a document, but I'm asking about the statements. They are eminently political. They are not constitutional. These people said that they had opted for war. Do you have that in your report, who was in favour of war, who caused the war? Provoked the war.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I talk a great deal about the events that led up to war. Not trying to be careful not to, you know, isolate it to either a single statement or a single event, because I basically reject this notion which I think is implicit in a lot of your questions that there is a linear predetermined road to conflict from which there seem to be no -- no human volition to stop it from -- from moving forward. I would like to look at the broad spectrum of causes and events that did, in fact, lead to war, and I tried to do that. I think there are a lot of things that I did, in fact, not include that should be noted. I did not, for example, talk much about the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution, which was the source of great distrust of Serbia and Milosevic in the period from 1989 on. I did not mention -- I think I mentioned in passing the removal of weapons by the Yugoslav People's Army from the Territorial Defence forces in May of 1990, which caused so much anxiety about the intentions of the JNA amongst the various republics. I think -- you know, one could certainly look at my report and say there are factors that are not there, and I would agree. I think the effort that I made was to include what I thought were the most significant and relevant factors leading to the outbreak of war. I did not attempt to assess the constitutionality or legality of those matters. I did report when one party or another contended that there was unconstitutionality or illegality in these various acts, but as I said, that was just a routine litany presented by the various parties to the conflict in order denounce the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you've taken me back to the 17th of May, 1990, now, when the Presidency -- or, rather, the JNA decided to put under control the weapons -- under its control the weapons of the Territorial Defence. That's what you had in mind, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you think that the JNA did not have the right to do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's a good question. My understanding of the way the hierarchy worked was that they did, but I -- there may be constitutional issues or legal issues in there which would suggest the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, there are no such things. If so, show us. Was the Territorial Defence subject to the JNA, or, rather, under the control and command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that the Territorial Defence reported to the JNA and to the Ministry of Defence of the various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we can look at the English version. This is Josip Boljkovac. We don't need the other version. We saw him at the beginning when he said that the Serbs would no longer be what they were, but obviously he wasn't in favour of war. So may we just look at the English version, have the English version up on our screens. That will suffice. "[In English] All Serbs and Yugoslavia were under attack, not Croatia." [Interpretation] Says he. "[In English] In the exclusive interview, Franjo Tudjman's internal affairs minister Josip Boljkovac admitted Croat leadership carried out planned attacks on Croatia Serbs in 1991 in order to start a war. 'Tudjman wanted the war at any cost following the concept according to which Serbs must disappear from Croatia,'" [Interpretation] Boljkovac said. Now, this probably relies upon what Tudjman said. We could have done without war. "[In English] Croat war time leader Franjo Tudjman wanted the war at any cost." [Interpretation] Did you take into consideration the fact that a civil war and the events that take place during a civil war are determined by the nature of a civil war and that we have to ask ourselves who wanted war and could a war have been avoided?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What -- what publication is this from? I'm sorry, I don't see the title of the publication or -- it's from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was taken from the internet, Mondo, text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But just out of curiosity, Mr. Karadzic, why do the English version and B/C/S version contain different pictures referring to different internet address? One refers to Mondo. The other refers to "Oslobodjenje."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This interview was given to the daily Sudwest [phoen] from Frankfurt, and then it was broadcast by the various agencies and summarised or shortened, but the main passages remain intact. I can read the Serb version if you like or the English. "During the testimony Glavas accused me of persecuting him because he destroyed the bridge on the river Drava in Osjek. He claimed he had destroyed the bridge to protect the town from the JNA tanks, and I responded and said that at the time the JNA was a regular army of an internationally recognised state while Croatia, which was not recognised, was part of Yugoslavia. Then I explained who started the armed conflicts in that part of Slavonia." And this entire interview was published and carried in the different media and agencies, but the substance of it is that Mr. Boljkovac confirmed that it was Croatia who wanted the war, and did you take that into account in your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this article before. It's apparently an interview given in 2009. Is that right? Yes. I guess I wouldn't know exactly what to make of it, because it does appear that he references here some testimony at a trial in which he was testifying against a former mayor, and so that may have, may have, influenced what he said here. I really wouldn't -- let's say it doesn't meet my highest standards in terms of document reliability, or least I can't determine that it does without checking some of this a little bit more. So did I take it into account? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, does that mean that I now have to have reservations towards your testimony, because you're actually testifying on behalf of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that you have a number of reasons to be -- to have reservations about my testimony. I would expect that. I am testifying in response to an invitation of the Prosecution and, let's say, a commission by the Prosecution to prepare the report. I'm not really testifying on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Mr. Donia, just say yes or no when I ask you this: Did you know that Izetbegovic and Tudjman acknowledged that they consciously opted for the war option?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've secured, you know, the -- established that, that Tudjman made such a statement. I need to see Izetbegovic's statement to agree that he stated exactly as you put it here, which is to consciously opt for the war option. I don't think it's quite that -- quite that explicit. Again, if you can show me the document, I'm happy to acknowledge its -- its content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me tell that we will be producing this document where he said, "We could have done without a war, but then we would have stayed within Yugoslavia." He said that on television Sarajevo on the 15th of February, 1993. [In English] We made our choice, and we could have easily done it differently. The price we paid is high, but it had to be paid. If I am to be blamed for it, then Karadzic should not. We could have avoided this conflict had we remained united as Yugoslavia, but we wanted independence. Towards the end of 1991, we established a Patriotic League in order to prepare for war." [Interpretation] And so on. That was published in different writings, the transcript of that statement of his, but we'll deal with that later. Let us now link this up with the proposal that was being prepared by the federal parliament in order to find a legal way to secede. Actually, there was a law that was being prepared for legal secession. Do you see that now? The federal parliament is preparing a way that would allow legal secession. Tudjman and Izetbegovic avoid that in order to go to war. Why is that not included in your reports, that they wanted to go to war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without seeing the document, the quotation that you just read and contended was by Mr. Izetbegovic did not say what you said it did. That was that he consciously opted for the war option. He talked about preparation for war, not consciously opting for the war option. Now, that was a misrepresentation on your part of what that citation said, which is why I'm asking you to show me documents that say what -- what you -- what you contend they say or what you're proposed to suggest that they say. And I think I've explained that included in the reports are a wide variety of things that are said by various parties. I think I've presented the information on, for example, the formation of the Patriotic League and the Council for National Defence of the SDA. I view that as a significant factor in the preparation for and lead-up to war, and tried to describe, to some points anyway, the position of the -- of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These did not make it into my corpus of things that I chose to cite to analyse the sources of the war. I believe they were not representative of the policies that were pursued. They certainly are not represent of -- representative of a conscious desire for war. I don't think anybody had a conscious and deliberate desire for war until perhaps the very last minute in this. I don't believe you did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, this interview of Josip Boljkovac's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness didn't confirm anything about the content of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right then. We'll deal with it some other time. 1D1408. Could we have that again, but now it is 13.35 -- at 13.35, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Because we said if Yugoslavia does not break up peacefully there's going to be one hell of a civil war. It nevertheless broke up non-peacefully. It broke up through the unilateral declaration of independence by Slovenia and Croatia and the seizing by these two countries, republics, of their border posts, which was an act of force and which was an act that was in violation of the Helsinki principles. But the European powers and the United States ultimately recognised Slovenia and then Croatia and then Bosnia as independent countries as member -- and admitted them to the United Nations. The real problem was that there was a unilateral declaration of independence and a use of force to gain that independence rather than a peaceful negotiation of independence, which is the way it should have happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's US Secretary of State James Baker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was Secretary of State at the time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was Secretary of State at the time of the recognitions, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we keep this same number, but from 46:17. Let us see what another high US official has to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "When we finally went ahead and recognised, one of the reasons we did so was because it had become a major domestic political issue for us here. We have particularly a large Croatian American community, and Mr. Bush lost most of them in the election that he lost because they were unhappy with our having delayed as long as we did in recognising Croatia. "While German actions encouraged the armed secession of ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you see that this was a purely political issue, a domestic political issue related to the elections, and that Mr. Eagleburger is aware of the fact that it was unlawful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't concur that what you just showed me establishes that. He -- this is, first of all -- these are very carefully selected excerpts from statements by, as I indicated, many different public figures in the crisis which are deliberately selected, apparently, in this -- in this video to make a particular point, and that means it's really, I think, a Serb propaganda film. The statement that he made, I think you can see the problem with this, that the US policy as it was being carried out on the scene by the ambassador in Belgrade, the embassy in Belgrade, was very remotely, if at all, related to domestic political considerations. The US position over this time I would call quite consistent from the time of Baker's visit to Belgrade in June of 1991 in which he was clearly in favour of preserving Yugoslavia and the changes that occurred in the next couple months were -- introduced a great deal of doubt, I think, into American policy or American policy-makers' minds about the wisdom of this. So I don't -- I don't accept your characterization of what he said. I don't think it's what he said, and would just acknowledge that he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us leave US domestic policy aside now and let us leave aside what is a good thing to do in politics or not. But James Baker did say that it was unlawful because it was one-sided and violent, breaking up a country and it's borders that had been guaranteed by the Helsinki final act and the constitutions of the republics and the constitution of the SFRY. So did Baker not confirm here that it had been illegal? So is that Serb propaganda?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, these excerpts? The number is the same, but the minute references are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have noted the end time for each, but I take it there's -- there's no objection from the Prosecution? They will be admitted separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D252 and D253 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, let me ask you, on the 17th of May, 1990, the Yugoslav People's Army placed under its control the weapons of the Territorial Defence. Do you agree that that was done in a lawful way? Actually, you agreed to that already, but do you agree that they did that because they were in fear that the secessionist republics would create their own armies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the republics have the right to establish their own armies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had the right to have a Territorial Defence force and a police force and a reserve police force. They didn't have the right to form a new separate army, to my knowledge, but they -- they had plenty of military forces, in fact, at their disposal when this whole thing started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D36. Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Donia, that Izetbegovic, at a very early stage already in the spring of 1991, said that he would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia and that he would not sacrifice the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the sake of peace? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'd like to see the specific document, and if you could tell me what the provenance of this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript of the session of the joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think that this was already in February 1991. This is very important, a very drastic statement, and it was received with a great deal of bewilderment everywhere. Did you include this statement in your report? The 27th of February, 1991. A month after the joint government had been established.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at a -- it looks like a partial translation of a partial quote, and I -- I'd like a minute to review this or get the entire thing at least before the applause line there. I don't know that this is a representation of the entire statement that he made. It looks like it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's huge the entire transcript, but this is the fourth joint session, only the fourth joint session of the joint Assembly. The 27th of February. It's in EDS -- or, rather, we have the page numbers here. If you wish, we can get the entire transcript, but this is his statement, and in the Serbian version you can see the original transcript. He said: "However, these two things that I mentioned here a sovereign and integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, a peaceful path to achieving it, are for me not on the same scale in terms of value. For a sovereign Bosnia I would sacrifice peace. For peace in Bosnia I would not sacrifice a sovereign Bosnia ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go on. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in this, what he had stated. Were you aware of the fact that already in February 1991 he said that even at the expense of sacrificing peace he would go for a sovereign Bosnia? P969 is the Prosecution number, right? 969?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm just asking you to go one sentence further and get this entire statement. I'm not asking for the whole transcript or the entire speech even. I'm just asking that where you cut off this translation, in the middle of a sentence, that you can continue it to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't see it very well. It says: "Likewise, because --" oh, I see, just a moment, please. "Likewise, because that is also, I don't know what, the subject of polemics. On that scale of values, if I had to choose, for me Bosnia comes first and then Yugoslavia. That's the way things are for me." However, either -- it's not Bosnia or Yugoslavia that is my point, it is sovereignty or peace.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my point is you shouldn't take this out of context. You should be representing this statement which is, I think, an integral statement in which he shows some balance between these two considerations, that if you just read the first part alone is not there. So I think it's important to have the entire statement viewed in -- in the context that he's kind of groping for a way to say this that does, in fact, state emphatically his commitment to Bosnia and puts the commitment to Yugoslavia in second place, as well as to talk about the relationship between war and sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll adjourn for today here. Doctor, you have access to those minutes or transcripts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's dated 17th of February, 1991. So overnight you may have the opportunity to read those parts and come back again. There are a couple of matters briefly. As for the -- Mr. Tieger, this extended sitting in -- on or in the week of the 21st, I have noted some vacant slot in the courtroom, so there seems to be no reason why that cannot be done if necessary. So we will request the registry to mark the courtroom for -- for our use if necessary, in the future, on those days. And the -- secondly, the request from the Defence for their experts to be present for the -- for the coming -- the Prosecution expert witnesses. Subject to our ruling on the motion which is still pending, it is the -- the Defence request is consistent with the practice of the Tribunal and our guideline. We'll grant them. I should have noted that the Prosecution didn't oppose it. We'll rise, and we will resume tomorrow at 2.15 but at Courtroom III, not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
